posts.hook: How to introduce an anxiety coat to a rescue dog who doesn't trust new things yet.
posts.body:
Slide 1: How to introduce the Settle Coat slowly — for the dog who needs slow.

Slide 2: Day 1. Don't put it on. Leave it near his bed so it smells like the room. That's all.

Slide 3: Day 2–3. Drape it over him while he's already settled — on the sofa, after a walk. Let him wear it for two minutes. Remove it before he asks you to.

Slide 4: Day 4–5. Do up one fastening only. Keep the session short. Pair it with something good — a chew, a lick mat, a quiet sit-together.

Slide 5: Day 6 onward. Build up the time gradually. The goal is that he stops noticing it's there. That's when it's working.

Slide 6: This is what the handwritten guide in every Steady Hound box covers. Because a nervous dog doesn't need a new thing pushed on him — he needs a reason to trust it.

posts.hook: Three things rescue dog owners wish they'd known before buying an anxiety wrap.
posts.body:
Slide 1: Three things worth knowing before you buy an anxiety coat — from the owners who've already been through the drawer.

Slide 2: 1. Fit matters more than pressure. A coat that bunches, slips back, or gaps at the chest doesn't apply consistent pressure — and inconsistent pressure is worse than none. Check the chest measurement against a breed-specific sizing guide, not just weight.

Slide 3: 2. Don't put it on for the first time during a trigger. If the first time your dog wears it is at a fireworks display, you've paired the coat with the worst moment. He needs to wear it on boring Tuesdays first.

Slide 4: 3. It's not instant. Most dogs need several sessions across a week before they stop registering the coat. The ones who seem to respond straight away are usually already in a lower state of arousal than you think.

Slide 5: The handwritten guide in every Steady Hound box covers all of this — because a rushed introduction undoes everything a well-made coat can do.

What the coat, the bed, and the feeder do is give a nervous dog more ways to cope — a layer of physical reassurance during a trigger, a place he chose to decompress after, a feeder that slows down the stress-eating that often goes alongside high arousal.

A dog who has these things is not 'fixed.' He's a dog with better tools. That's a meaningful difference.

And yes — even with two weeks to go before bonfire night, a slow introduction across seven to ten days is possible. The handwritten guide in every box walks you through it.
